strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem setting: prior-free motion extrapolation from multi-view video, positioned explicitly against reconstruction-centric dynamic 3DGS methods and physics-prior methods (PINN/simulation-based).

Strong empirical gains on the intended task: on the NVFi Dynamic Objects and Indoor Scene benchmarks, ParticleGS substantially outperforms reconstruction baselines (e.g., ~38.2 vs ~30.9 PSNR for Shark extrapolation, ~33.6 vs ~28.2 for Whale) and beats both extrapolation baselines (NVFi, GSPrediction) in most scenes, while remaining competitive in reconstruction.

Evaluation uses benchmarks designed for extrapolation (NVFi, PanopticSports) rather than repurposing novel-view-synthesis datasets, and the authors acknowledge metric subtleties (extrapolation metrics can exceed reconstruction metrics under sparse test views).

Quantitative ablations (Table 4) support the core design choice: removing the dynamics latent state causes a large drop (e.g., 17.6 vs 37.6 PSNR reconstruction on Dynamic Objects), and qualitative results (Figs. 3-6) show more stable future trajectories than baselines.
Code release is claimed and the appendix provides implementation details (encoder/ODE/decoder sizes, optimization schedule), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate and largely compositional: the method combines InstantNGP hash encoding, a PointNet/Point-BERT-style neighborhood encoder, a Neural ODE over a global latent vector, and MLP heads producing affine deformations. No component is new, and the 'particle dynamics system' framing is mostly conceptual packaging.

The claimed contribution of 'learning differential equations describing the dynamics' is overstated. The ODE evolves only the global feature g_t while the local feature l is time-invariant (z_t = (g_t, l)), so individual Gaussian particles do not have genuinely evolving per-particle dynamics; the extrapolated motion is driven by a single global latent trajectory decoded through affine transforms. This weakens the paper's core narrative versus, e.g., per-particle Neural ODEs.

The ablation undermines two of the three claimed contributions: 'w/o Neural ODE' (33.790 vs 34.224 extrapolation PSNR) and 'w/o Affine Deformations' (33.886 vs 34.224) show only marginal differences, i.e., the ODE solver and affine decoder contribute very little beyond a plain regression baseline; only the latent state matters, and what remains is close to a standard deformation-field model with a global latent code.

Extrapolation of chaotic or partially observed motion is inherently ill-posed, but the paper offers no analysis of failure modes, prediction uncertainty, or how far beyond the training window the model remains valid; the deterministic formulation gives no mechanism for modeling multi-modal futures (the arg max p(I|past) framing in Eq. 3 is heuristic).

Baseline coverage on the real-world dataset is thin (only Grid4D and GSPrediction on PanopticSports), and no runtime, memory, or training-cost comparison is reported despite the framework involving FPS/KNN regrouping, a transformer, and ODE integration.

Numerous presentation and consistency issues that should not appear at submission: a missing code URL ('Our code is available at' ends mid-sentence), inconsistent naming ('ParticalGS' vs 'ParticleGS'), 'Grid' instead of 'Grid4D', references to 'Figure 4.1' when the overview is Figure 2, grammatical errors ('Figure 3 visually comparison results'), and the affine decoder details deferred entirely to the appendix.

Some quantitative claims are overstated in the text (e.g., '~0.1 higher PSNR than Grid4D' on Fan/Telescope is within noise, and the ~0.3 dB average improvement over GSPrediction on PanopticSports is modest), and several reconstruction results (Fallingball, Dining Table) are notably worse than the best baseline without a convincing explanation.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful and underexplored problem: prior-free temporal extrapolation of dynamic 3D scenes, going beyond the interpolation focus of most dynamic 3DGS methods.

The evaluation covers the purpose-built NVFi extrapolation benchmarks (6 dynamic objects + 4 indoor scenes) plus a real-world PanopticSports subset, comparing against both reconstruction baselines (HexPlane, TiNeuVox, 4D-GS, DeformGS, Grid4D) and extrapolation baselines (NVFi, GSPrediction).

On the NVFi synthetic benchmarks the extrapolation results are substantial (e.g., Shark extrapolation PSNR 38.17 vs. 30.90 for Grid4D; Gnome House 31.17 vs. 24.09 for NVFi), and the ablation confirms that removing the latent dynamics state causes a large degradation.

The paper is transparent about its evaluation protocol (timestamp splits, known metric confounds between reconstruction and extrapolation) and includes a limitations section acknowledging the lack of cross-scene generalization.
weaknesses: The core technical framing is misleading. The paper claims each Gaussian carries a per-particle dynamics state, but Equation 6 shows z_t = (g_t, l) where the local features l are static and only a single global feature g_t evolves through the Neural ODE. The 'dynamics' of the entire scene is thus one shared latent trajectory, which is closer to a global temporal conditioning signal than a learned particle dynamics system. This is a material weakness, not just presentation: scenes with independently moving objects (multiple trajectories, interactions, contacts) are not actually modeled as interacting particles, and no experiment tests this.

The 'prior-free' claim is overclaimed. The affine decoder decomposes the transformation into rotation, scaling, shearing, linear velocity, and nonlinear terms (Appendix A.1), which is itself a hand-designed structural prior. Meanwhile the 'first end-to-end prior-free extrapolation method' claim ignores GSPrediction [56], which also requires no physical priors.

The empirical support for the claimed contributions is weak. The ablation (Table 4) shows that removing the Neural ODE module or the affine deformations barely changes results (e.g., extrapolation PSNR 33.790 vs. 34.224 without the ODE; 33.886 vs. 34.224 without affine deformations on Dynamic Objects). This undercuts the paper's two central design claims; essentially only the latent conditioning matters, and the paper does not explain what the 1-layer ODE actually learns beyond what a simple MLP over time would.

Reconstruction quality is highly inconsistent across scenes (e.g., Fallingball reconstruction PSNR 21.05 vs. 34.90 for NVFi; Bat 21.05 vs. 47.03 for DeformGS), and extrapolation PSNR sometimes exceeds reconstruction PSNR by large margins (Fallingball: 21.05 reconstruction vs. 27.56 extrapolation). While the authors attribute this to sparse viewpoints, it suggests the metrics do not cleanly separate dynamics accuracy from appearance fitting, weakening the headline 'significantly outperforms in extrapolation' claim.

On the real-world PanopticSports dataset, gains over GSPrediction are marginal (~0.3 PSNR average) and the method loses on several entries (Tennis extrapolation, Football LPIPS, Basketball SSIM/LPIPS). The strongest comparisons are confined to the synthetic NVFi datasets.

The claimed learned 'differential equations' are never analyzed. No trajectory visualization, physical plausibility check, or comparison of latent dynamics against ground-truth motion is provided, so it is impossible to verify the central claim that the model learns dynamics rather than simply extending a smooth latent interpolation.

Presentation is careless in ways that affect credibility: the abstract's code URL is missing ('Our code is available at' with nothing following), the method overview is cited as 'Figure 4.1' (a nonexistent reference), Figure 1 is cited as 'As shown in 1', Equation 3 is cited as 'definition 3', and the method name is misspelled as 'ParticalGS' in the conclusion and Table 4. The appendix section titled 'Additional quantitative results' actually contains only qualitative figures.
Reproducibility is uncertain: no functional code link, and key design details (how the affine matrix decomposition is enforced, how many FPS centers/neighborhoods) are deferred or unspecified.

strengths: The paper addresses a clearly motivated and underexplored problem—prior-free future frame extrapolation for dynamic 3D scenes—positioning it against both reconstruction-only methods (HexPlane, TiNeuVox, 4D-GS, DeformGS, Grid4D) and physics-informed methods (NVFi) and GNN-based extrapolation (GaussianPrediction).

The extrapolation results are substantial and consistent: e.g., on the NVFi Dynamic Objects dataset ParticleGS improves extrapolation PSNR from ~26-30 dB (best baselines) to ~34-38 dB (e.g., Shark 38.17 vs 30.90 for Grid4D; Whale 33.60 vs 28.25), and it also wins on most Dynamic Indoor Scene extrapolation metrics (e.g., Chessboard 29.34 vs ~22.6 for NVFi), while remaining competitive on reconstruction.

The experimental breadth is good: two synthetic NVFi benchmarks plus the real-world PanopticSports dataset, with both reconstruction and extrapolation metrics reported, and a reasonable discussion of why reconstruction and extrapolation metrics can diverge.

An ablation study (Table 4) supports the central design choice: removing the dynamics latent state causes a large drop (~17.6 vs ~37.6 PSNR on Dynamic Objects), and removing the Neural ODE or affine decoder causes smaller but consistent degradation.

The modular pipeline (latent dynamics encoder → Neural ODE evolution → affine decoder) is well-motivated, and implementation details (RK4 solver, FPS/KNN grouping recomputation policy, training schedules) are provided, plus a public code release promise supporting reproducibility.
Qualitative results (Figures 3-6) with zoomed detail crops convincingly illustrate that baselines drift or blur during extrapolation while ParticleGS maintains object localization and detail.
weaknesses: The framing as a 'particle dynamics system' is overstated. Only the global feature g0 evolves through the Neural ODE (Eq. 6); the local features l are static and shared by all time steps. Per-Gaussian dynamics are therefore not individually modeled—the learned 'dynamics' is a single global latent trajectory decoded affinely—so the claimed connection to classical particle dynamics (where each particle has its own evolving state vector) is weaker than the text suggests.

The ablation undercuts the importance of two claimed contributions: removing the Neural ODE module and removing affine deformations only changes extrapolation PSNR by ~0.3-0.4 dB (34.22 vs 33.79/33.89) on Dynamic Objects. Nearly all benefit comes from the latent state representation, which raises questions about whether the ODE-based evolution module is the key ingredient or a marginal one. A comparison against a simpler time-conditioned decoder or GRU-style temporal model would strengthen the case.

Technical soundness of the decoder (Eq. 7) is questionable: additive rotation R' = R + ΔR does not preserve orthonormality of the rotation matrix, and S' = S + ΔS can produce negative or degenerate scales. The appendix mentions decomposing A into components, but the main-text formulation as written is not physically/numerically clean, which conflicts with the paper's 'physically plausible motion' motivation.

The novelty claim ('first end-to-end, general dynamic 3D extrapolation method without manually defined physical priors') is too strong: GaussianPrediction [56] is also a prior-free learned extrapolation method (GCN-based), and the individual components (multi-resolution hash encoding, PointNet/attention global pooling, Neural ODEs, affine deformation fields) are all established; the contribution is primarily an architectural combination rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Extrapolation horizons are short (training up to t=0.75, testing to t=1 on NVFi; ≤0.9 vs >0.9 on PanopticSports). There is no analysis of long-horizon extrapolation behavior, error growth over time, or robustness to motion regimes not represented in training—properties the ODE framing is supposed to enable. The acknowledged caveat that NVFi extrapolation metrics can exceed reconstruction metrics also complicates interpretation of Table 1/2.

Reconstruction quality is sometimes clearly below the best Gaussian baselines (e.g., Shark 39.96 vs Grid4D 40.75, Fallingball 21.05 vs Grid4D 47.44 — though baselines also degrade there), and Table 3 omits most reconstruction baselines; comparative breadth on PanopticSports is thinner than on the synthetic sets.

Presentation issues that should be corrected: the paper alternates between 'ParticleGS' and 'ParticalGS'; Figure 2 label 'Dynamics latent state ecoder'; text refers to 'Figure 4.1' (Section 4.1) instead of Figure 2; 'achieves ~0.1 higher PSNR than Grid' should presumably read 'Grid4D' and 0.1 appears implausibly small (Table 1 shows ~1.8-2.1 dB); the code URL is truncated in the abstract; several references ([8], [14], [58]) lack venues/years. These do not affect the science but reduce polish.

Cost/efficiency reporting is limited: no training time, memory, or rendering speed comparison against the strong Gaussian baselines, despite the FPS/KNN/attention machinery added on top of 3DGS, which is a practical concern for adoption.

strengths: The problem formulation is well-motivated and clearly articulated: time-conditioned deformation models memorize timestamp-to-state mappings and fail at extrapolation, while ParticleGS conditions rendering on an evolved latent physical state (Eq. 2 vs. Eq. 3). The toy experiment in the supplementary (2D damped spiral, Fig. 6) concretely illustrates why learning a derivative field enables extrapolation where time-conditioned curve fitting fails.

The factorized physical state encoding (Eq. 4) is a sensible and effective design: particle-level static features plus F shared system-level dynamic fields reduce evolver complexity from O(NG) to O(FG). The ablation (Table 4, rows 1, 2.1–2.3) supports the design: removing factorization increases GPU memory without performance gain, and F=8 is a good trade-off.

The empirical evidence is broad and strong: four datasets (Dynamic Object, Dynamic Indoor Scene, Dynamic Multipart, real-world FreeGave-GoPro), covering reconstruction and extrapolation, with consistent best or near-best results (e.g., ~2.5–5 dB extrapolation PSNR gains over TRACE/FreeGave on synthetic data, and consistent gains on real-world data). Baseline selection is appropriate, spanning time-conditioned, physics-prior (NVFi, GaussianPrediction), and velocity-field (TRACE, FreeGave) methods.

Ablations are comprehensive and well-targeted, isolating the encoder factorization, number of dynamic fields, Neural ODE evolver (largest degradation when replaced by MLPs), physical decoding, progressive training, and neighborhood regularization. Rendering speed (Table 3) shows the framework remains practical despite the ODE integration.

Training details are sufficiently specified (supplementary: 14-d input features, network dimensions, RK4 solver, progressive schedule, densification handling via neighborhood regeneration) to support reproducibility, and the paper honestly reports limitations (cannot extrapolate motions deviating from learned dynamics).
weaknesses: The central 'physics-based' claim is under-supported beyond the inductive-bias argument. The Neural ODE learns an arbitrary latent transition function; nothing verifies that the learned dynamics correspond to actual physical laws (no comparison to ground-truth governing equations, no physical-quantity interpretation of the F fields beyond a qualitative RGB visualization in Fig. 3). The paper conflates 'continuous-time latent state evolution' with 'learning physical laws', and the Markov-property argument (Sec. 3.1) is asserted rather than demonstrated — a learned latent state is Markovian by construction, which does not by itself imply physical fidelity.

The extrapolation protocol (train on first 75%, test on last 25%) may partly reward methods that capture smooth/periodic motion continuation rather than genuine out-of-distribution physical prediction. There is no evaluation of generalization to new initial conditions, longer-horizon rollouts, or error growth over extrapolation horizon, which would directly test the 'learned physics' claim.

Two baseline rows in Table 6 (TRACE: Gnome House 22.968/0.642/0.351 vs. Chessboard 22.969/0.642/0.352, and correspondingly identical extrapolation numbers) appear copy-duplicated across different scenes, raising a data-reporting concern that should be corrected and verified.

Some modeling choices are physically inconsistent or under-justified: the decoder rotates positions about the scene origin via x_t = x + Rod(R)x + T (Eq. 10), which is not a rigid-body rotation about a particle center; notation is also inconsistent ('r_t = r ◦ δr' described as quaternion product while R is predicted as an axis-angle vector and handled by Rodrigues' formula). The claimed connection to Material Point Method is loose — shared dynamic fields are more akin to a low-rank motion-mode decomposition (e.g., DynMF [23]) than MMP-style physics.

Comparison breadth is limited in places: FPS is reported only for two datasets and only against velocity-field methods; wall-clock training time and memory for the Neural ODE integration are not reported; and the strongest physics-prior competitors are compared on only a subset of datasets for Table 2.

Novelty is moderate in isolation: Neural ODEs for particle dynamics [6,20,36,41], latent dynamics from videos [4,15,31], and motion-mode factorizations [23] all exist; the contribution is primarily their combination and adaptation to 3DGS extrapolation rather than a fundamentally new technique.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and clearly defined problem: temporal extrapolation of dynamic 3D scenes beyond the observed window, as opposed to interpolation-only novel view synthesis. The problem formulation (Sec. 3.1) distinguishing time-conditioned deformation D(P,t) from state-driven evolution D(P,Zt) is clear and easy to follow.

Empirical results are extensive and consistent: evaluation on four datasets (Dynamic Object, Dynamic Indoor Scene, Dynamic Multipart, FreeGave-GoPro), including a real-world dataset, with full per-scene numbers in the supplementary (Tables 5-8). The reported extrapolation gains over time-conditioned baselines (e.g., ~9 dB over DeformGS on Dynamic Object) and ~2.5 dB over velocity-field methods (TRACE, FreeGave) on synthetic data are substantial.

The ablation study (Table 4) is reasonably thorough, covering the factorized encoding, number of dynamic fields F, ODE vs. MLP evolver, physical decoding, progressive training, and neighborhood regularization, and the reported component contributions are mostly consistent with the design narrative.

The supplementary material includes a didactic toy experiment (2D damped spiral) that convincingly illustrates why time-conditioned fitting fails at extrapolation while derivative-based integration can succeed, plus sufficient implementation detail (architectures, FPS/k-NN settings, training schedule) to support reproducibility.

The factorized state design (F shared dynamic fields vs. N particle states, Eq. 4) is a sensible efficiency contribution, and the claimed O(NG) to O(FG) complexity reduction is supported by the FPS results in Table 3.
weaknesses: The central 'physics-based / prior-free physical laws' framing is overstated and not substantiated. Nothing in the method enforces or verifies any physical law: the Neural ODE learns an unconstrained neural vector field over 16-dimensional latent features, and the decoder predicts arbitrary translations/rotations. There is no evidence (e.g., recoverable Newtonian quantities, conservation properties, or comparison to known ground-truth dynamics) that the learned fields correspond to physical laws rather than a generic smooth latent dynamics model. The paper essentially shows that a smooth, low-dimensional, continuous-time latent ODE extrapolates better than high-capacity time-conditioned deformers - a plausible inductive-bias effect, not demonstrated 'physical reasoning'. The abstract and Fig. 1 claims ('Learn physical laws of motion') go beyond what is shown.

The Markov/spatiotemporal-awareness argument (Sec. 3.1, comparing Eq. 2 and Eq. 3) is conceptually shaky. A time-conditioned model is also a deterministic function of t within the observed window; the difference is purely architectural inductive bias. Moreover, the initial state Z0 is encoded only from the canonical (t=0) Gaussians, so all future evolution must be fully autonomous - the paper does not discuss how this handles partially observed motion initiation or non-stationary scenes, and it concedes in the limitations that dynamics deviating from training cannot be predicted, which weakens the practical case for 'learning physics'.

Real-world gains are marginal. On the FreeGave-GoPro dataset the extrapolation improvements over FreeGave/TRACE are small (e.g., 26.789 vs. 26.510 PSNR, 0.15 vs. 0.16 LPIPS in Table 2; on several scenes in Table 8, e.g., Wrist Rest and Pen2, ParticleGS is not the best method). The headline claims rest largely on synthetic benchmarks whose motions (rigid objects, pendulum-like fan, orbiting satellite) are exactly the regimes where a smooth latent ODE prior is expected to shine.

Ablation design has inconsistencies that undermine confidence: the 'w/o FE' row (1) is run on a different GPU (A6000 48GB) and is missing entirely for the Dynamic Indoor Scene dataset; F=16 actually outperforms the chosen F=8 on the Dynamic Object dataset (36.552 vs. 36.471), so the hyperparameter selection criterion is unclear; there is no training-time or training-memory comparison to baselines, only rendering FPS.

The evidence that improvements stem from 'high-order dynamics' rather than the strong smoothing of the F-dimensional field bottleneck is not disentangled. A simple ablation constraining TRACE/FreeGave or DeformGS to a similar low-rank latent motion space is absent; without it, the attribution of the 2.5 dB gain to Neural ODEs and 'higher-order physics' is speculative, even though Table 4(3) shows ODE > MLP.

Evaluation breadth on extrapolation is limited: the held-out period is only the last 25% of frames following NVFi/FreeGave protocols, so no results on longer-horizon rollouts where ODE integration error would compound, and no analysis of how far beyond T extrapolation quality degrades.

No code release is mentioned, and the method has many interacting pieces (progressive training schedule, densification-coupled neighborhood regeneration every 500 iterations, FPS keypoint counts differing per dataset), which raises reproducibility concerns despite the detailed appendix.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly positioned: replacing time-conditioned deformation with an evolved latent physical state (Encoder–Evolver–Decoder) is a sensible reframing of dynamic 3DGS, and the supplementary toy experiment (damped spiral, Fig. 6) gives an intuitive demonstration of why time-conditioned models fail to extrapolate while a learned ODE does not.

The factorized state design (Eq. 4) is technically sound: evolving F shared system-level dynamic fields instead of N particle states reduces evolver complexity from O(NG) to O(FG), and the ablation (Tab. 4, row 1) empirically supports this design choice, showing memory reduction without accuracy loss.

The experimental evidence is unusually thorough: four datasets spanning synthetic objects, compositional indoor scenes, multi-part objects, and real-world GoPro captures, with full per-scene results in the appendix (Tabs. 5–8) rather than only aggregate numbers.

Consistent and substantial quantitative gains: extrapolation improvements of ~3–7 dB PSNR over both time-conditioned baselines (DeformGS, Grid4D) and physics-prior baselines (NVFi, GSPrediction), and ~2.5 dB over the strongest velocity-field methods (TRACE, FreeGave), while also achieving the best reconstruction on most datasets — the gains are not confined to one dataset or metric.

The ablation study isolates each component (factorized encoding, number of fields F, ODE vs. MLP evolver, physical decoding, progressive training, neighborhood regularization), and the ODE-vs-MLP comparison (row 3) directly supports the central claim that continuous-time dynamics modeling matters.

Engineering details that matter for 3DGS practice are addressed: handling changing Gaussian counts via densification/pruning, online regeneration of neighborhood patches, and a progressive training schedule to stabilize ODE-based optimization.
Rendering speed (Tab. 3) is competitive with velocity-field baselines, showing the ODE formulation does not destroy real-time rendering.
weaknesses: The central 'physical' framing is asserted more than demonstrated. The evolver is a generic neural ODE over latent fields with no explicit physical constraints, inductive bias, or validation that the learned dynamics correspond to any known physical law (e.g., no recovery of gravity/damping parameters, no divergence/energy diagnostics, no experiments on systems with known equations of motion). The paper's own argument that latent first-order systems can represent 'any high-order dynamics' (Eq. 6–7) equally implies it can represent purely non-physical memorization. The claim of 'learning physical laws' therefore rests on extrapolation accuracy alone.

The evolver in Eq. 8 takes an explicit time argument, f_evolver(g_t, t), which partially undermines the Markovian/time-invariant-law argument made in Sec. 3.1: a time-dependent derivative function reintroduces exactly the timestamp dependence the paper criticizes, and could in principle learn time-conditioned memorization through this channel. No ablation or analysis addresses this.

The Markov-property motivation is questionable for the tested scenes. Real-world human–object interaction (FreeGave-GoPro Box/Collision/Pen) is not Markovian in the Gaussian state, since future motion depends on unobserved forces (the human hand); extrapolating such scenes 'following learned physical laws' is physically ill-defined, and the paper does not discuss this limitation despite strong reported numbers there.

Evaluation horizon is modest and uniform: all extrapolation experiments use a train-on-first-75%/test-on-last-25% split following prior work. There is no analysis of error growth over longer horizons, which is precisely where ODE integration error compounding versus memorization behavior would differ — the setting that would most convincingly support the physics claim.

Evidence of physical plausibility is mostly qualitative. Beyond PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, the paper offers rendered comparisons (Figs. 4–5, 7–12) and an RGB visualization of latent states (Fig. 3) whose interpretation ('dynamic coherence', 'temporal stability') is not quantified against any ground-truth physical quantity.

Ablation conditions are not fully consistent with the main table: ablation row (1) was run on a different GPU (A6000/48GB vs. RTX 4090) and omits the Indoor Scene dataset, and there is no variance/seed reporting anywhere despite the small deltas that decide some rankings (e.g., Table 2 margins of ~0.1–0.3 dB).

The decoder only evolves position, rotation, and scale (Eq. 10); spherical harmonic coefficients and opacity are not driven by the state, so appearance changes in the future are not modeled — an acknowledged but under-examined limitation for extrapolation over 25% of a video.

Training cost and GPU memory of the full model relative to baselines are not reported (only the ablation's memory remark), making efficiency claims harder to assess; several baseline numbers appear to be quoted from prior papers rather than retrained, which the paper does not state explicitly.
Minor: the Fast Fourier of claims ('Newtonian or Navier–Stokes', Sec. 1) is never tested with any fluid scenario; all experiments are rigid/deformable solid-like motion.
